newsitem.title: DENMARK: SOCCER-COACHES SHUN "GOLDEN GOAL", PLEAD FOR MORE SUPPORT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-COACHES SHUN "GOLDEN GOAL", PLEAD FOR MORE SUPPORT.

text.p: Europe's national coaches are against deciding matches with sudden death extra time, apart from Czech Dusan Uhrin, trainer of the only side to have lost the final of a senior competition with such a "golden goal".
The controversial sudden death issue and a need for more support of national team trainers by clubs emerged as main concerns on the first day of the UEFA national coaches convention on Monday.

"They discussed things like the golden goal and they're almost all against it. Even Berti Vogts, who won the European championship with the golden goal, doesn't like it," said the European soccer body's technical director Andy Roxburgh.
"Dusan Uhrin, who is the only one to lose with the golden goal, is for it. It's a paradox," the former Scotland manager, who organised the convention, told a press briefing.

Roxburgh said the golden goal, which decided the Euro 96 final won by Vogts's Germany in June, was a key topic during discussions about the increasing complexity of a national team coach's job and the intense pressure under which he works.

When pressed as to whether the golden goal would be kept for the 1998 World Cup finals, UEFA general secretary Gerhard Aigner said though coaches might dislike it, players probably prefered it to the risk of missing in a penalty shootout.
"We have to convince teams to decide games in 90 minutes," he said.
"We need more protection for national team players as to their availability for official matches," said former France coach Gerard Houllier, a guest speaker at the convention.

He said UEFA wanted to see the world body FIFA's ruling that players be made available for competitive internationals five days before the match strictly adhered to. The deadline for friendlies should also be increased from two to three days.
Englishman Roy Hodgson, former Switzerand coach now in charge of Internzionale of Italy, said the discussions aimed to help UEFA and FIFA find ways of improving the game.
"Countries' football is their top clubs in competition and also their national teams. Kids aspire to play for their country," said Hodgson.

FIFA official Walter Gagg said as he came out of the session that the analysis of both Houllier and Hodgson had been very frank and that they had not held back where they felt the need to be critical of players or teams.

But Hodgson said of the sterile football at Euro 96 that "all coaches approach the game the only way possible. As things are now you won't see any cavalier football at the highest level when the only thing that counts is the result.
"Domestic progammes destroy international players before a national coach even gets them," he said.

Gagg, who is close to FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter, said unofficial discussions outside the convention about the problem of settling drawn matches had included an idea to play a full 30 minutes of extra time but the first team to score earned the golden goal, worth double in the event of a draw.
Aime Jacquet, in charge of 1998 World Cup hosts France, was forced to miss the convention after being rushed to hospital with a kidney complaint at the weekend, Roxburgh said.
